extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, patent practitioners, USPTO officials, patent stakeholders (inventors, universities, corporations)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and explanation of proposed statutory reforms in the Patent Reform Act of 2007, including goals, specific legislative changes, and the practical legal effects on patent prosecution, patentability, litigation, damages, and harmonization with foreign systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional purpose of patent law
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional purpose: to ‘promote the progress of science and useful arts’ by granting limited exclusive rights to inventors in exchange for disclosure of inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent system has two objectives: (1) encourage inventors via limited exclusive rights; (2) require disclosure and a limited monopoly term so the public benefits and future inventors can use the invention after the monopoly expires. (Citation to U.S. Const. art. 1, Sec. 8.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter and statutory bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents issue to inventors of new and useful inventions or improvements; basic statutory provisions cited include 35 U.S.C. Sec. 101 (patentable subject matter), Sec. 102 (novelty), and Sec. 103 (non-obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability is measured against statutory standards of novelty and non-obviousness; the Report references these statutes as the baseline legal standards that reforms must respect or clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve patent quality and application process (legislative goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: One primary goal of the Act is to improve patent quality and the patent application process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee frames reforms to ensure issuance of high-quality patents through procedural and substantive changes to examination, applicant obligations, and USPTO authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address litigation cost, delay, and uncertainty (legislative goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary goal is to improve and clarify aspects of patent litigation to reduce excessive costs, uncertainty, and delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms aim to create less expensive and more expeditious alternatives for resolving validity issues and to adjust rules on damages, willful infringement, venue, and appeals to reduce litigation burdens and encourage settlements where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization with international patent systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the U.S. patent system more consistent with other industrialized nations where useful (e.g., move away from unique first-to-invent rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonization addresses costs and complexity faced by applicants who file abroad and seeks to align the U.S. with global norms (e.g., objective filing-date focus), while preserving beneficial U.S. features such as a one-year grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change to a first-inventor-to-file priority system
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 replaces the U.S. first-to-invent rule with a ‘first-inventor-to-file’ system that makes filing date the most relevant date for priority while preserving a one-year grace period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new system eliminates interference proceedings (priority fights over who invented first) and instead uses derivation proceedings to ensure the filer is a true inventor; filing date/objective date simplifies prior art determinations and encourages prompt filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a one-year grace period for inventor disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act retains a one-year grace period during which an inventor’s own disclosure (and disclosures by others based on the inventor’s information) will not be prior art against the inventor’s application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee stresses importance to universities and small inventors: grace period affords time to prepare applications and obtain funding and promotes early public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a USPTO administrative ‘derivation’ proceeding to resolve disputes about whether the first person to file was actually the true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation replaces interference proceedings for priority disputes; it focuses on whether the filer derived the invention from another rather than who invented first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Because priority is based on filing date under the new system, costly and complex interference proceedings (to determine who invented first) are eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference proceedings historically took years, cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, required discovery, and imposed document-retention burdens on applicants; their elimination reduces cost and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify prior art rules by emphasizing filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art will be measured largely from the filing date (an objective date) rather than the uncertain date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides predictability: filing date is listed on the patent/application and avoids uncertain, corroboration-dependent invention-date inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant responsibility to search and prepare high-quality applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that applicants must bear responsibility to search the state of the art and prepare high-quality patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report notes questions whether USPTO fees and funding reflect the work necessary for high-quality examination and whether applicants are doing adequate prior art searches and preparing high-quality filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorize USPTO to require patent searches with explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act authorizes the USPTO to require patent searches with explanations when an application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change is intended to improve examination quality and reduce issuance of low-quality patents by obliging applicants to provide searching and explanatory information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of applications and third-party submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for eventual publication of all applications and enhance the utility of third parties’ submissions of relevant information regarding filed applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased publication and third-party inputs aim to improve examination by exposing examiners and the public to relevant prior art earlier in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) / administrative validity review
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a relatively efficient and inexpensive administrative system for resolution of patent validity issues before the USPTO and establish the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee expects an administrative alternative to litigating validity issues to be quicker and less costly than district-court litigation, addressing the lack of viable administrative review at present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codify and clarify damages and willful infringement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Codify and clarify the standard for calculating reasonable royalty damage awards, as well as awards for willful infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report warns against statutory language that would pluck limited factors from case law and impose rigid tests; it emphasizes proper burden assignment and clear standards of proof rather than requiring massive macroeconomic analyses in every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of burdens in reasonable royalty analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current caselaw, the burden of apportioning the base for reasonable royalties falls on the infringer; the burden for applying the Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR) falls on the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report criticizes proposals that would change burdens or impose rigid requirements on courts, noting that apportionment is often not a complex issue under current law and that misplaced burdens would increase complexity and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid statutory provisions that mandate massive damages trials or unclear burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Report identifies as a shortcoming any bill language that would require complex macroeconomic analysis and massive damages trials in every case without assigning burdens or standards of proof to appropriate parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes would be costly, time-consuming, increase litigation delays, spur years of litigation over phrase meanings, and discourage settlements; thoughtful assignment of burdens and standards is required if change is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve venue and appellate review of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve venue rules in patent cases and provide for appeals of claim construction orders when warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reforms are aimed at reducing forum-shopping and clarifying interlocutory review opportunities to reduce uncertainty and litigation strategy abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give USPTO fee-setting authority and end fee diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant the USPTO the ability to set its fees and end congressional ‘fee diversion’ so fees reflect necessary work and fund examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate fee-setting is presented as necessary to equip the USPTO to handle increased and complex application volumes and to improve patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codify and improve inequitable conduct doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Codify and reform the doctrine of inequitable conduct to address plaintiff-focused litigation concerns and uncertainty in enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report notes testimony was not uniform on how to reform inequitable conduct but identifies codification and clarification as a goal to reduce abuse and unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give USPTO Director discretion to accept late filings in certain instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the Director of the USPTO discretion to accept late filings under specified circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change provides administrative flexibility to address equitable situations without burdening courts or unduly penalizing applicants for technical failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove residency restriction for Federal Circuit judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove the residency restriction for judges on the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structural change intended to broaden the pool of qualified judges eligible to serve on the Federal Circuit; included among the Act’s systemic reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorize limited liability adjustments for certain non-patent matters (e.g., Check 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include provisions limiting patent liability for institutions implementing the ‘Check 21’ program (and similar narrow protections where warranted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are narrowly tailored statutory provisions intended to avoid unintended patent exposure for certain government-authorized programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make technical and transitional amendments and set effective dates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act includes necessary technical amendments and provisions setting effective dates for reforms (e.g., transition to first-inventor-to-file).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These catch-all measures ensure smooth implementation and address detailed statutory harmonizations required for the larger reforms to function.
